source: Klein, Calderwood, Clinton-Cirocco (2010) Rapid Decision Making on the Fire Ground: The Original Study Plus a Postscript (JCEDM 4(3))
finding: Primary abstract of the edited 1985 study gives the sample and the headline split. Commanders were interviewed about one nonroutine critical incident each. Most decision points were handled by direct identification of a typical situation and a typical action; few showed option comparison.
numbers: 26 fireground commanders, mean experience 23 years. 156 decision points probed. Under 12% showed simultaneous comparison and relative evaluation of two or more options. Over 80% were direct identification of situation as prototype plus typical action.
quote: In less than 12% of them was there any evidence of simultaneous comparisons and relative evaluation of two or more options.
limits: Only the abstract (via Crossref) was read, not the full text or the postscript commentary. The abstract says 'over 80%', not '80-90%'. The remaining share (up to about 8%) is not described in the abstract. Coding was done by the authors; no inter-rater figure seen.
agent_relevance: Confirms the K01 figures at the primary source. S0 can cite 'over 80% of decision points' and not '80-90%'.

source: Klein, Calderwood, Clinton-Cirocco (1986) Rapid Decision Making on the Fire Ground (Proc. HFES 30(6))
finding: The 1986 conference version defines the method as a critical incident protocol analysis and defines the comparison test: simultaneous comparison and relative evaluation of two or more options. Same under-12% finding; RPD model proposed.
numbers: Under 12% of decision points showed comparison. No sample size in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only (Crossref). 'Comparison' is defined as simultaneous relative evaluation, so sequential single-option evaluation does not count as comparison. That makes the 12% figure narrow.
agent_relevance: Tells us what 'no comparison' means: the commander tested options one at a time. An agent that checks one option then moves on is still RPD-style by this definition.

source: Klein et al. (1988) ARI Technical Report 796 via DTIC ADA199492; SAGE page for the 2010 version
finding: Full text of the founding report could not be opened. DTIC PDF and SAGE page both returned HTTP 403 to curl and WebFetch.
numbers: No numbers read. Crossref lists the DTIC record without an abstract.
limits: Gap 1 stays partly open: the breakdown of the 156 decision points (the share between 'over 80%' and 'under 12%'), any inter-rater check, and the postscript text were not read.
agent_relevance: Do not quote a figure for the unaccounted share. Say 'up to about 8% not described'.

source: Grove, Zald, Lebow, Snitz, Nelson (2000) Clinical versus mechanical prediction: a meta-analysis (Psychological Assessment 12(1))
finding: Abstract confirmed through Europe PMC. Mechanical (formal, statistical) combination of data was about 10% more accurate than clinical combination on average. Clinical judges were often as good, rarely clearly better.
numbers: About 10% more accurate on average. Mechanical substantially better in 33%-47% of studies, depending on the analysis. Clinical substantially better in only 6%-16% of studies. Advantage held across task, judge type, judge experience. Clinical did relatively worse when interview data were among predictors.
quote: Mechanical-prediction techniques were about 10% more accurate than clinical predictions.
limits: The count '136 studies' is not in the abstract and stays unverified here. Abstract only. Human health and behaviour tasks, not LLM work.
agent_relevance: Confirms the 10% figure. Supports a G rule: when a simple scored formula exists for the task, do not let the quick judgment override it.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree (American Psychologist 64(6))
finding: Full text not reachable: the open copy at a university host did not resolve. Only the Semantic Scholar one-line summary was seen: the quality of an intuitive judgment depends on how predictable the environment is and on the person's chance to learn its regularities.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Metadata only, so K06's two conditions still rest on earlier lines (a26, b05, b28) rather than the source read this session.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 premise stands on the review's two conditions; the new evidence below tests whether a model can sense them.

source: Chen, Ang, Cusin, Fava, Pizzagalli (2025) Exploring Task Design and Heuristics Interaction Through a Knowledge-Free Option Generation Task (PMC13400725)
finding: A task with no domain knowledge contradicts take-the-first. First-generated paths were less unique than later ones, and the most unique paths came late. The paper also summarises the long-term working memory (LTWM) side: later options better in nurses and soccer players.
numbers: 44 healthy adults and 53 analysed MDD patients. Uniqueness of first vs later paths, median 122.7 vs 374.5 (healthy) and 155.7 vs 542.0 (MDD); both p<0.001. Path-index effect 0.184 healthy and 0.249 MDD. It cites Ward et al. 2010 (nurses) and 2013 (soccer) as LTWM-consistent, Belling et al. 2015 as time pressure shifting toward TTF-like behaviour, and Missier et al. 2015 as first-accessible options giving poorer outcomes.
limits: Read through a page summariser, not line by line. Outcome is uniqueness, not decision quality. Knowledge-free task, so it is off the take-the-first scope (familiar, ill-defined tasks). Authors say the time limit may explain the gap.
agent_relevance: First option is not reliably best outside sport. Keep S0 as a default and add the later-option check for novel tasks.

source: Johnson & Raab (2003) Take The First; Raab & Johnson (2007) Expertise-based differences in search and option-generation strategies
finding: Primary papers are closed access. The Johnson & Raab and Raab & Johnson numbers (samples, effect sizes for first vs later option quality) could not be opened. Only a one-line summary was seen: Raab & Johnson extend the handball option-generation findings and give a model of option generation, deliberation and selection.
numbers: None read. Gap 3 effect sizes remain unknown.
limits: Metadata and secondary description only. The secondary source (d06) lists them as the origin of take-the-first and as supporting 'less is more' (more options, lower mean quality).
agent_relevance: Do not state a quality gap number for take-the-first in the schema.

source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) NDM prompts for LLM triage (PMC13061108), re-opened for baselines
finding: Re-read for the chain-of-thought question. The only control is a plain prompt asking for a classification. There is no 'think step by step' arm and no token or cost comparison. The authors say the gain may partly reflect the extra reasoning before the answer in non-reasoning models.
numbers: Plain prompt: 'Please give a triage classification for the following vignette.' RP prompt names the recognition-primed model and asks to match typical cases then simulate; DF prompt asks to construct, question and reframe a frame.
limits: Only the first 100,000 of 132,941 characters read. Single domain. Authors state it is unclear whether findings generalise.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open: no equal-token test of NDM frames against plain chain of thought exists in anything opened. Run it ourselves on two or more task types.

source: Yang et al. (2025) Dynamic Early Exit in Reasoning Models (DEER)
finding: Reasoning models often contain a correct answer early. A confidence rule at reasoning transition points lets the model stop early without training. Confidence threshold 0.95 was used across 11 models and 10 datasets; accuracy held in the range 0.9-0.97.
numbers: About 75% of AIME24 samples contain a point where early exit gives the right answer. 60.8% of correct MATH-500 samples and 35.1% of correct GPQA samples stay correct after only 20% of reasoning steps. Across 11 reasoning models and 10 benchmarks: chain length cut 19.1% to 80.1%, accuracy up 0.3 to 5.0 points. Code tasks compress less (average 19.9% vs 61.5% for math and science). Threshold set too low gives a sharp accuracy drop; too high exits late.
limits: Open-weight reasoning models only. Some baselines fail on QwQ-32B because its end-of-thinking token is unreliable (DEER still cut 19.1%). Harder sets give smaller savings.
agent_relevance: A concrete S0 early-exit rule: sample a trial answer at a reasoning boundary, exit if its confidence passes a high threshold (about 0.95), else continue. Expect much less saving on hard and code tasks.

source: Liu & Wang (2025) Answer Convergence as a Signal for Early Stopping in Reasoning
finding: On math tasks models settle on their final answer after about 60% of reasoning steps. Three stop rules were tested on five benchmarks and five open models: stop when the answer repeats, raise the end-of-thinking probability, or a learned stopper. Simple rules work on easy tasks and get unstable on hard ones.
numbers: Convergence after about 60% of steps on math. On NaturalQuestions, answer-consistency stopping cut tokens by over 40% and raised accuracy. Learn-to-Stop cut tokens 44% on GSM8K with QwQ-32B (755.1 to 418.9) and 46.2% (R1-Qwen-7B) to 47.7% (R1-Qwen-32B) on NQ. Larger models stabilise earlier.
limits: Open-weight models only. Unsupervised rules were 'less stable' on MATH-500 and GPQA, per the paper's own wording. Exact accuracy deltas per cell not copied.
agent_relevance: Cheap rule for S0: stop when the answer is the same across the last few checkpoints. Use it on easy tasks only; use a learned or verified stop on hard ones.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Know When They're Right: Probing Hidden States for Self-Verification
finding: A probe on hidden states predicts whether an intermediate answer is correct, with good calibration, and can predict correctness before the answer is written. Used as an exit rule it saves tokens. The signal appears in long-chain reasoning models and degrades in short-CoT models.
numbers: ROC-AUC above 0.7 and ECE below 0.1 in distribution. R1-Distill-Qwen-32B over 0.9 ROC-AUC on AIME. Tokens cut 24% with no loss. Probes trained on math transfer across MATH and GSM8K but not stably from logic to math, and are less calibrated on AIME.
limits: Needs hidden-state access, so not available to a text-only API agent. Open-weight distilled models.
agent_relevance: Shows the model has a better internal correctness signal than it voices, but a text-only agent cannot read it. Use sampled-answer agreement as the text-only stand-in.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) When More Thinking Hurts: Overthinking in LLM Test-Time Compute Scaling
finding: Extra thinking tokens help at first and then hurt, and the turning point depends on difficulty. Easy problems peak early; hard ones keep gaining. Past the crossover, answer flips go from wrong-to-right to right-to-wrong.
numbers: R1-32B: early gain +3.2% per 500 tokens; marginal utility turns negative beyond about 12K tokens. Easy problems (levels 1-2) peak at about 1.5K tokens; hardest (level 5) benefit up to about 8K. Flip ratio (negative/positive) passes 1 near 7K tokens; at 8K the 95% CI is [1.21, 1.68]. Accuracy drop from 12K to 16K tokens -0.9% (95% CI [-1.4, -0.4]). Of 80 manually checked negative flips, 67.5% were real overthinking (a correct answer rejected). Combined detector (hesitation words, answer oscillation, confidence drop): r=0.82 with overthinking, 76.3% precision at 80% recall. s1-32B crosses earlier (5K).
limits: Two open reasoning models (R1-32B, s1-32B), budget forcing by appending 'Wait'. Preprint. Math difficulty scale. Which dataset fed each panel was not fully clear from the text.
agent_relevance: Gives a difficulty-keyed compute rule and a text-only overthinking detector (answer oscillation). The S0 first answer is more often final on easy items; keep it if later rounds merely reconsider it.

source: Dang et al. (2026) The First Impression Problem: Internal Bias Triggers Overthinking in Reasoning Models (ICLR 2026)
finding: Reasoning models form a quick guess before reasoning. When that guess conflicts with later reasoning, they reflect more. Removing the question text after the first reasoning step cuts redundant reasoning; injecting a wrong bias raises it.
numbers: Removing the question after the first step cut length by 31.1% to 53.5% (reduction ratio r) across datasets. Bias injection with wrong guesses lengthened reasoning and correct guesses shortened it (Table 3; values not copied). Several overthinking-mitigation methods did not remove the effect.
limits: Open-weight reasoning models, complex reasoning tasks. Table 3 values not copied exactly.
agent_relevance: Direct machine analogue of recognition-then-check: the quick guess exists, and conflict triggers the slow loop. Supports logging first guess vs final answer.

source: Kadu & Krishnan (2026) ReflexGrad: Within-Episode Failure Recovery via Progress-Gated Dual-Process Routing
finding: A fast refinement step every k=3 steps and a slow causal-diagnosis step that fires only when m=5 consecutive low-progress scores appear. Over-triggering (m=3) costs accuracy and calls; never firing (m=10) misses recoveries.
numbers: ALFWorld 134 tasks, 10 seeds. Qwen-3-8B 35.1% to 75.4%; GPT-5 46.3% to 88.1%. Trigger m on GPT-5: 3 gives 84.3%, 5 gives 88.1%, 7 gives 86.6% (per-setting table read; worst setting 84.3%). Each unnecessary slow activation costs 5 LLM calls plus a 5-step cooldown. Evaluator false-positive rate under 3%, so false-trigger bound about 0.15 over 5 draws. m=10 gave missed recoveries.
limits: One benchmark (ALFWorld), author-built router, several comparison methods re-implemented by the authors. The false-alarm accuracy cost is small (3.8 points between best and worst m tried).
agent_relevance: Stall-based trigger (no progress for about 5 steps) with a cooldown is a tested text-only escalation rule. False alarms cost calls and some accuracy but did not break the agent.

source: Wang et al. (2023) SwiftSage (arXiv 2305.17390), trigger conditions re-read
finding: SwiftSage switches from the fast module to the slow one when any of four hand-set conditions fire: stuck, invalid action, critical decision, unexpected observation. It returns to fast mode when the planned action buffer is empty.
numbers: Stuck means K=5 consecutive steps with zero reward. Other triggers: fast module's action invalid; action is a critical decision such as giving a final answer; observation shows an exception. Two consecutive invalid or failing planned actions revert to the fast module.
limits: Main text shows no ablation of the individual triggers; the ablations read concern prompt design, not triggers. A learned switch is listed as future work. So there is no evidence for which trigger matters most.
agent_relevance: Start with these four triggers for the text-only agent and log which fires; per-trigger value is still unknown.

source: Saxena & Upadhyay (2026) Nudgeability: Reasoning Models Follow Confidence Signals Without Tracking Their Own Competence
finding: Inserting one sentence of confidence or doubt into otherwise identical reasoning changes whether the model answers or calls a tool, but the change is badly aimed: the models do not delegate more on problems they cannot solve.
numbers: Nine open-weight reasoning models (Qwen, Gemma, GLM), two tasks: median confidence-to-doubt swing 20.6 percentage points. Larger provider-served models: 53 to 70 points. Median 42% of induced flips are well-targeted, only a +2 point median lift over random selection.
limits: Preprint. The signal is an inserted sentence, not the model's own natural confidence, so it tests use of the signal rather than its validity. Outcome is delegation to a tool, not answer correctness.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: in-context confidence words move behaviour strongly but barely track competence. Do not let the agent's stated confidence alone gate escalation; use task-regularity checks and agreement of repeated samples.

source: Hsiao (2026) Rethinking Verbalized Confidence for LLM-as-a-Judge
finding: On post-2025 frontier proprietary models, verbalized confidence beats log-probabilities as a soft score for judging, with an overconfidence advisory and self-debate added. Older models paid an accuracy cost for the same additions.
numbers: Up to 18 LLMs across GPT, Claude, Gemini families on SummEval, AggreFact, HelpSteer2. No single headline number copied from the abstract.
limits: Only the abstract and first page read. Judging text quality, not answering tasks. Single author, preprint.
agent_relevance: Counterweight to d16: on newer models, spoken confidence can carry some signal. Needs a test on our own model, per task type.

source: Naeini et al. (2023) Large Language Models are Fixated by Red Herrings: OnlyConnect Wall dataset (NeurIPS D&B)
finding: Puzzle walls with built-in red herrings are hard for LLMs far beyond what a non-misleading version is. Removing the red-herring structure raises scores a lot, which fits a fixation or Einstellung account.
numbers: Humans solved 285 of 494 walls and 1405 of 1976 groups. GPT-4 0-shot solved 6 walls and 239 groups on the original set; on the randomised set (red herrings removed) about 59 walls and 595 groups; on the WordNet set 471 walls and 1926 groups. Best few-shot GPT-4 about 3 to 7 walls. GPT-3.5 0-shot 0 walls, 114 groups. Task-2 connection-naming F1 41-45% vs about 80% human.
limits: Table layout in the extracted text was jumbled; the GPT-4 0-shot randomised and WordNet values are read from the final row and should be re-checked. The synthetic sets differ in more than red herrings. 2023 models only.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a familiar-but-wrong grouping can block a better one in LLMs, but it is not a test of a forced re-look step.

source: Haq, Chhaya, Pandey, Bhattacharya (2025) Is your LLM trapped in a Mental Set?
finding: A small test of mental set (DeCaro maths-equivalence design) on three LLMs. Results are weak and mixed. Few-shot plus zero-shot chain of thought made models use more steps than the one-step shortcut humans use.
numbers: Six problems per condition. Exact match, few-shot: GPT-4o 0.33 (shortcut) / 0.66 (shortcut after complex) / 0.66 (complex) / 0.83 (complex after shortcut); Llama-3.1-70B 0 / 0.16 / 0 / 0.66; Llama-3.1-8B 0.16 / 0 / 0 / 0. With CoT, steps were 3 in every cell.
limits: Six items per cell, so differences of one item (0.16) are noise. No test of a re-look prompt. Order effects are not a clean Einstellung penalty.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open: no Einstellung penalty size and no forced re-look test for LLM agents were found. Design our own: familiar-but-worse option present vs absent, with and without a forced second look.

source: Wang & Sun (2025) Unable to Forget: Proactive Interference Reveals Working Memory Limits in LLMs Beyond Context Length
finding: When earlier values for the same key are in context, retrieval of the latest value falls log-linearly toward zero as the number of overwritten values grows, even though the answer sits right before the query. Telling the model to ignore earlier updates helps little.
numbers: Accuracy declines log-linearly with interference load across models (no single cut-off number copied). Prompt fixes gave marginal gains.
limits: Retrieval of updated values, not simulation of a causal system. No direct test of a 3-variable, 6-transition cap.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analogue to the human limit on mental simulation: tracking many state updates costs accuracy. Keep the simulate branch short and write state out each step.

source: Gong (2026) Language Models Share a Readout Bottleneck in Working Memory
finding: LLMs show the human N-back signature: accuracy falls as load N rises and errors cluster on lures. Attention finds the target; the limit is reading it out under interference from other items.
numbers: 15 pretrained LLMs from three families, 70M to 14B parameters, plus small transformers trained from scratch. Linear probes decode target-versus-lure almost perfectly even on false alarms. Sharpening attention gave negligible gains; suppressing identity of non-target items improved d' in nearly all model-by-load conditions.
limits: Models up to 14B and letter N-back, far from frontier agents and from real simulation tasks.
agent_relevance: Supports a working-memory style cap in LLMs, but the exact numbers (3 variables, 6 transitions) have no direct LLM counterpart yet. Gap 8 partly answered: a load limit exists; its size for the simulate branch is unmeasured.

source: Kim & Schuster (2023) Entity Tracking in Language Models
finding: Tracking the contents of boxes after a series of move/put operations works only in models trained on code (GPT-3.5 code-davinci-002 and later), and accuracy depends on how many operations affect a box.
numbers: Plots accuracy against 0-7 operations affecting a box for Flan-T5 base/XL, GPT-3 davinci and text-davinci-003 vs a random baseline; no single figure copied. The task fixes 12 operations per scenario.
limits: 2023 models. Exact accuracy values were not extracted from the figure text. Which models succeeded was taken from the abstract.
agent_relevance: Background for gap 8: state-tracking depth is a measurable property, so the simulate-branch cap can be measured on our own model by varying operations per variable.

source: Maliha & Kabir (2026) LLMs for Cardiovascular Risk Prediction from Structured Clinical Data
finding: Plain statistical models beat prompted LLMs on structured data. Logistic regression and random forest were well ahead of zero-shot LLMs and ahead of few-shot LLMs.
numbers: 1,190 records, 11 attributes. Accuracy: logistic regression 84.1%, random forest 92.8%, XGBoost 92.3%, SVM 87.8%. Gemini zero-shot 60.0%, 15-shot 80.0%; GPT zero-shot 66.7%, 15-shot 73.3%. LLM test set looks like about 30 cases (recall 93.3% fits 14 of 15), so the LLM numbers are very noisy.
limits: Small LLM test set (size inferred, not stated). Compares models, not human clinicians, so it is not a replication of Grove.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: only a weak signal that LLM judgment loses to a simple formula on structured features. Keeps the Grove-style rule plausible but unproven for LLM judges.
